newsitem.title: USA: Dollar closes sharply higher vs Europe in US trade.
newsitem.headline: Dollar closes sharply higher vs Europe in US trade.

text.p: Buoyed by strong U.S. economic data and dollar-supportive comments from a German official, the dollar closed near two-year highs versus the mark, the Swiss franc and the French franc on Monday, dealers said.
The dollar also jumped higher against the yen, moving above the 114 threshold for the first time in almost a month and coming close to matching a 42-month late-October high of 114.92 yen.

"There was just outright dollar buying across the board and it just snow-balled on itself because a lot of people who hadn't expected the move were not positioned for it," said Marc Chandler, a senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The dollar closed at 1.5555/60 marks, up from 1.5415/18 at the open, but slightly off from Monday's 23-month high of 1.5590.
After reaching a 23-month high of 1.3280 Swiss francs, the U.S. currency closed at 1.3210/20 francs, up from 1.3118/28 at the open.
Against the French franc, the dollar ended at 5.2720/50, after touching a 22-month high of 5.2805 French francs.
The dollar ended the session at 114.48/58 yen, up from an opening price of 113.65/75.
Traders said the impetus for the dollar's strong move came from Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing and November manufacturing data from the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM).
The NAPM's headline index rose to an unexpectedly strong 52.7 reading in November against 50.2 in October, suggesting continued firm growth in the U.S. manufacturing sector.

Meanwhile, the Bundesbank's Issing told a bankers' forum in Germany on Monday that one of the possible effects of the approach of Europe's single currency union was a shift out of the deutschemark into dollar-denominated investments.
"It was the Issing remarks more than anything else that got us started," said Kevin Lawrie, global foreign exchange manager at Pittsburgh-based Mellon Bank N.A.
The remarks reinforced a dollar rally kindled late last week and over the weekend, when French and German central bank officials began talking actively about their desire for a stonger dollar.
In order to meet strict convergence criteria for Economic and Monetary Union, many European countries have been forced to observe strict fiscal and monetary discipline despite struggling economies.
As a result, many European Union members are hoping that weaker currencies can fuel export-driven growth, and keep their economies on an even keel.
"Every single central banker and politician in Europe seems to want a stronger dollar," said Robert Fullem, assistant vice president at Natwest Bank Plc.
In addition to the European push for a firmer dollar, Fullem said that strong demand for surging U.S. stocks and bonds has also played a role in the U.S. currency's rise.
In other trade on Monday, the dollar ended at Canadian $1.3510/15, virtually unchanged from C$1.3512/17 at the open. The British pound was lower at $1.6799/04, down from $1.6847/57 at the open.
The Australian dollar ended virtually unchanged at $0.8162/67 versus $0.8161/66.
